You are helping a user write SQL queries to a database. If something is not clear, you can ask the user to clarify what they need. The schema for the database being accessed is the following:
        
CREATE TABLE employee (
    Employee_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Age INT,
    City TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Employee_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE shop (
    Shop_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Name TEXT,
    Location TEXT,
    District TEXT,
    Number_products INT,
    Manager_name TEXT,
    UNIQUE (Shop_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE hiring (
    Shop_ID INT,
    Employee_ID INT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Start_from TEXT,
    Is_full_time bool,
    UNIQUE (Employee_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Employee_ID) REFERENCES employee(Employee_ID),
    FOREIGN KEY (Shop_ID) REFERENCES shop(Shop_ID)
);

CREATE TABLE evaluation (
    Employee_ID TEXT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Year_awarded TEXT   PRIMARY KEY,
    Bonus REAL,
    PRIMARY KEY (Employee_ID, Year_awarded),
    UNIQUE (Employee_ID, Year_awarded),
    FOREIGN KEY (Employee_ID) REFERENCES employee(Employee_ID)
);

To pull “hard‑working employee” information, I need to know how you define **hard‑working** in this database. There’s no explicit “hard_working” column, so it’s usually inferred from **evaluation/bonus** (or tenure/full-time).

Here are common options—pick one (or tell me your rule):

### 1) Employees with the highest bonus (most “hard-working”) in a given year
```sql
SELECT e.Employee_ID, e.Name, e.Age, e.City, ev.Year_awarded, ev.Bonus
FROM employee e
JOIN evaluation ev ON ev.Employee_ID = e.Employee_ID
WHERE ev.Year_awarded = :year
ORDER BY ev.Bonus DESC;
```

### 2) Employees whose bonus is above a threshold (in a given year)
```sql
SELECT e.Employee_ID, e.Name, e.Age, e.City, ev.Year_awarded, ev.Bonus
FROM employee e
JOIN evaluation ev ON ev.Employee_ID = e.Employee_ID
WHERE ev.Year_awarded = :year
  AND ev.Bonus >= :min_bonus
ORDER BY ev.Bonus DESC;
```

### 3) Top N employees by total bonus across all years
```sql
SELECT e.Employee_ID, e.Name, SUM(ev.Bonus) AS total_bonus
FROM employee e
JOIN evaluation ev ON ev.Employee_ID = e.Employee_ID
GROUP BY e.Employee_ID, e.Name
ORDER BY total_bonus DESC
LIMIT :n;
```

### 4) Full-time employees (if you mean “hard-working” = full-time)
```sql
SELECT e.Employee_ID, e.Name, e.Age, e.City, h.Shop_ID, h.Start_from
FROM employee e
JOIN hiring h ON h.Employee_ID = e.Employee_ID
WHERE h.Is_full_time = 1;
```

Which definition do you want (top bonus / above threshold / top total / full-time), and do you want it **for a specific year** or **overall**?
Focus on the employee who got the highest one-time bonus.

```sql
SELECT e.Employee_ID,
       e.Name,
       e.Age,
       e.City,
       ev.Year_awarded,
       ev.Bonus
FROM evaluation ev
JOIN employee e
  ON e.Employee_ID = ev.Employee_ID
WHERE ev.Bonus = (SELECT MAX(Bonus) FROM evaluation);
```

If multiple employees tie for the highest one-time bonus, this returns all of them.
you should also make sure to get the name of the employee who meets the criteria

```sql
SELECT e.Employee_ID,
       e.Name,
       e.Age,
       e.City,
       ev.Year_awarded,
       ev.Bonus
FROM evaluation ev
JOIN employee e
  ON e.Employee_ID = ev.Employee_ID
WHERE ev.Bonus = (SELECT MAX(Bonus) FROM evaluation);
```
make sure to focus on the employee who got the highest bonus in that one-time category

```sql
SELECT e.Employee_ID,
       e.Name,
       e.Age,
       e.City,
       ev.Year_awarded,
       ev.Bonus
FROM evaluation ev
JOIN employee e
  ON e.Employee_ID = ev.Employee_ID
ORDER BY ev.Bonus DESC
LIMIT 1;
```
